HISTORY & PHYSICAL (DETAILED)

Consult Summary:
23-year-old woman with asthma and known peanut allergy developed rapidly progressive upper-lip swelling, throat tightness, dyspnoea, and dizziness ~30 min after eating prawn soup; clinician arranged emergency ambulance for suspected anaphylaxis.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Swelling of upper lip after eating prawn-containing soup.  
• Timeline:  
  – 19:00 today: Ate prawn soup.  
  – ~19:30: Noticed tingling and swelling at left corner of upper lip, then generalized upper-lip enlargement.  
  – Progressive increase in size; swelling “feels like it’s getting worse.”  
• Associated symptoms: Subjective throat tightness, difficulty breathing, possible chest tightness, dizziness.  
• Exacerbating/relieving factors: Triggered by prawn ingestion; no treatment taken prior to call.  
• Pertinent negatives: No antihistamine or epinephrine auto-injector available; no mention of urticaria or abdominal pain.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma – uses salbutamol inhaler PRN; no daily preventer.  
• Peanut allergy – childhood severe reaction requiring hospital care (~age 6).  
• Prior episode of facial swelling and breathing difficulty after Chinese food ~1 yr ago (no treatment details).  
• No other chronic illnesses mentioned.

Medications:
• Salbutamol inhaler – dose/route/frequency not documented (patient reports “regularly” uses).  
• Occasional “antihistamines” (names/dose/frequency not documented).  
Allergies: Peanuts (IgE-mediated); prawn/shellfish now suspected.

Social History:
• Lives with mother (present during call).  
• Social alcohol use (episode one year ago involved intoxication).  
• No smoking or recreational drug use mentioned.

Family History:
• Not discussed / not recorded.

Physical Examination:
• Vitals: Not recorded (remote consult).  
• General: Patient appeared increasingly distressed; visibly swollen upper lip.  
• Respiratory: Patient reports dyspnoea; no auscultatory findings available.  
• HEENT: Marked upper-lip swelling observed via video; no other findings documented.  
• Remaining systems: Not examined.  

Investigations:
• None performed in consult. Ambulance called for emergency evaluation.

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
Suspected IgE-mediated anaphylaxis secondary to shellfish (prawn) exposure with airway involvement.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. IgE-mediated anaphylaxis to shellfish – rapid onset after exposure, lip/throat swelling, dyspnoea, dizziness, atopic history.  
2. Isolated allergic angioedema – supports lip swelling; opposed by systemic symptoms (respiratory compromise, dizziness).  
3. Hereditary angioedema – recurrent swelling possible; opposed by clear food trigger and atopic background.

Issue 1: Suspected anaphylaxis
• Assessment: Progressive lip and likely airway swelling with respiratory difficulty and dizziness after prawn ingestion.  
• Plan:  
  – Emergency services (999) activated; patient instructed to remain with mother until ambulance arrives.  
  – Take available oral antihistamine while awaiting paramedics.  
  – Advise immediate hospital evaluation and treatment (likely intramuscular epinephrine, airway support, observation).  
  – Post-discharge: Arrange follow-up for allergy assessment, prescription and training for epinephrine auto-injector, asthma and allergy action plan.

Issue 2: Food allergies (peanut, probable shellfish)
• Assessment: History suggests multiple IgE-mediated food allergies.  
• Plan:  
  – Refer to allergy clinic for formal testing (peanut, shellfish, others).  
  – Education on food avoidance, label reading, emergency plans.  
  – Provide prescriptions for non-sedating antihistamine to keep on hand.

Issue 3: Asthma
• Assessment: Intermittent asthma; salbutamol only.  
• Plan:  
  – Review asthma control at follow-up; consider preventive inhaler.  
  – Reinforce inhaler technique and trigger avoidance.

General plan items:
• Provide written information on anaphylaxis recognition and management.  
• Encourage patient to inform friends/family of allergy action plan.  
• Follow-up via primary care within 1 week of hospital discharge or sooner if concerns.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: Objective vitals, full physical exam, medication doses, complete allergy list, family history.  
● No transcript–DDx conflicts identified.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; remote setting limited examination and vitals.
